result.markdown: --- title: "Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression" subtitle: "Equation · prediction · residuals · R² · centering · Topics 3–4 · Lab 2" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 1: regression models the **average outcome** as a function of predictors - Today: the simplest case — **one continuous predictor**, **one continuous outcome** - By the end you can: - write and read the equation, **in units** - **predict**, and know when to use a **confidence** vs a **prediction** interval - explain **residuals** and **OLS** without calculus - report **R²** and **adjusted R²** sensibly - **centre** predictors so the intercept means something ::: # Topic 3 — The straight-line model {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## The equation ::: {.eq} SBP~i~ = β~0~ + β~1~ × salt~i~ + ε~i~ ::: ::: {.incremental} - **β₀ (intercept)** — average SBP when salt = 0 - **β₁ (slope)** — change in average SBP for **each 1-unit increase** in salt (**mmHg per g/day**) - **ε (error / residual)** — everything else that makes person *i* differ from the line ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s2_simple_regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ## Fit it with `lm()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m1 <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g, data = ncd) summary(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = sbp ~ salt_g, data = ncd) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -41.857 -10.844 -0.434 9.888 55.093 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 107.4202 2.1490 49.98 <2e-16 *** salt_g 3.3893 0.2801 12.10 <2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 15.14 on 580 degrees of freedom (18 observations deleted due to missingness) Multiple R-squared: 0.2015, Adjusted R-squared: 0.2001 F-statistic: 146.4 on 1 and 580 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Read the Estimate column first. Then Std. Error, t, p. Then residual standard error and R². We will take each in turn today and in Session 3. ::: ## Interpretation — always in units ::: {.big .center} Each extra **1 g/day** of salt → mean SBP **3.4 mmHg** higher ::: ::: {.incremental} - "mmHg per g/day" — the slope carries **units of the outcome over units of the predictor** - This is a **crude** estimate (no other variables yet) — Session 3 adjusts it - It describes an **association across people**, not what happens if one person changes their diet ::: ## The unit you choose changes the number ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble( `Predictor unit` = c("per 1 g/day", "per 5 g/day", "per 1 SD of salt"), `Change in SBP (mmHg)` = round(b1 * c(1, 5, sd(ncd$salt_g, na.rm = TRUE)), 1) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 2 `Predictor unit` `Change in SBP (mmHg)` 1 per 1 g/day 3.4 2 per 5 g/day 16.9 3 per 1 SD of salt 7.6 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} Same model, same data — three different-looking numbers. Always report **the unit**, and pick an increment that is **clinically meaningful** (5 g ≈ a teaspoon of salt). ::: ## The intercept ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s2_simple_regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} No one in the survey eats 0 g of salt — the intercept is an **extrapolation**. Keep that in mind: we return to it under *centering*. ::: # Prediction {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Predict with `predict()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} new_salt <- tibble(salt_g = c(5, 8, 12)) predict(m1, newdata = new_salt) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 3 124.3668 134.5349 148.0922 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} "Adults who eat 8 g/day have a **mean** SBP of about 135 mmHg." ::: ::: {.warn} Predict only **within the range of the data** (about 2–14 g/day). Beyond it, the straight line is a guess. ::: ## Two different questions, two different intervals ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.key} **Confidence interval** "What is the **average** SBP of *all* adults who eat 8 g/day?" → uncertainty about the **line** ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.warn} **Prediction interval** "What SBP might the **next patient** who eats 8 g/day have?" → line uncertainty **plus** person-to-person scatter ::: ::: ::: ## CI vs PI in R: `interval =` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predict(m1, new_salt, interval = "confidence") |> round(1) # for the MEAN ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fit lwr upr 1 124.4 122.6 126.1 2 134.5 133.2 135.8 3 148.1 145.2 150.9 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} predict(m1, new_salt, interval = "prediction") |> round(1) # for an INDIVIDUAL ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fit lwr upr 1 124.4 94.6 154.2 2 134.5 104.8 164.3 3 148.1 118.2 178.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} At 8 g/day: mean SBP **135** (95% CI 133–136) but an individual may lie anywhere from **105** to **164**. ::: ## Both bands on one plot ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} grid <- tibble(salt_g = seq(2, 14, length.out = 100)) ci <- predict(m1, grid, interval = "confidence") |> as_tibble() |> rename(ci_lwr = lwr, ci_upr = upr) pi <- predict(m1, grid, interval = "prediction") |> as_tibble() |> select(pi_lwr = lwr, pi_upr = upr) bind_cols(grid, ci, pi) |> ggplot(aes(salt_g)) + geom_point(data = ncd, aes(y = sbp), alpha = .25, colour = col_blue) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = pi_lwr, ymax = pi_upr), fill = col_blue, alpha = .15) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci_lwr, ymax = ci_upr), fill = col_red, alpha = .5) + geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = col_navy, linewidth = 1) + labs(x = "Salt intake (g/day)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", caption = "Red = 95% CI for the mean · Blue = 95% prediction interval for an individual") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s2_simple_regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Notice the CI band is narrowest near the mean of salt and flares at the ends. The PI band is wide everywhere and contains roughly 95% of the dots. ::: # Residuals and OLS {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Fitted values and residuals ::: {.key} **Fitted value** ŷ = what the line predicts for a person. **Residual** = observed − fitted. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} augment(m1) |> select(sbp, salt_g, .fitted, .resid) |> head(5) |> mutate(across(everything(), ~ round(.x, 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 4 sbp salt_g .fitted .resid 1 131 6.9 131. 0.2 2 135 9 138. -2.9 3 127 5.8 127. -0.1 4 155 10.2 142 13 5 138 6.3 129. 9.2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s2_simple_regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ## OLS: choose the line with the smallest squared misses ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s2_simple_regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Each red square has side = the size of the residual; its area is the squared residual. OLS finds the intercept and slope that make the total red area as small as possible. No calculus needed: R does the minimisation. Axes are standardised only so the squares look square. ::: ## Residuals vs fitted: first look ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} augment(m1) |> ggplot(aes(.fitted, .resid)) + geom_point(alpha = .4, colour = col_blue) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_red) + geom_smooth(se = FALSE, colour = col_navy, method = "loess", formula = y ~ x) + labs(x = "Fitted SBP (mmHg)", y = "Residual (mmHg)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s2_simple_regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Residuals should scatter evenly around 0. Hold that thought — Session 4 reads this plot properly. ::: # R² and adjusted R² {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## R²: how much of the variation does the model account for? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} r2(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # R2 for Linear Regression R2: 0.202 adj. R2: 0.200 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sigma(m1) # residual standard error, in mmHg ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 15.13919 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - R² = **0.2** → salt alone accounts for about **20%** of the variation in SBP - **Residual SE ≈ 15 mmHg**: a typical miss — it is why the prediction interval is so wide ::: ## R² always rises; adjusted R² punishes junk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) junk <- as_tibble(matrix(rnorm(nrow(ncd) * 20), ncol = 20, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("z", 1:20)))) d_j <- bind_cols(ncd |> select(sbp, salt_g), junk) |> drop_na() map_dfr(c(0, 5, 20), \(k) { f <- reformulate(c("salt_g", head(names(junk), k)), "sbp") s <- summary(lm(f, data = d_j)) tibble(`random noise variables added` = k, R2 = round(s$r.squared, 3), `adjusted R2` = round(s$adj.r.squared, 3)) }) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 `random noise variables added` R2 `adjusted R2` 1 0 0.202 0.2 2 5 0.21 0.201 3 20 0.227 0.198 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Adding pure noise **raises R²** every time; **adjusted R²** charges for each extra parameter. Use adjusted R² when you compare models of different size. ::: ## Reading R² sensibly {.smaller} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.good} **A low R² does not mean the predictor is unimportant** BP depends on age, genes, diet, stress… A salt slope can be real and clinically important with R² of 0.2. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.bad} **A high R² does not mean the model is right** A model can fit well and still violate assumptions, or fit *this* dataset only (overfitting). R² says nothing about causation. ::: ::: ::: # Topic 4 — Centering and scaling {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## An intercept at age 0? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_age <- lm(sbp ~ age, data = ncd) coef(m_age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) age 96.3162078 0.7430034 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} The intercept says: a **0-year-old** has SBP **96 mmHg**. Our sample is aged 30–69, so this describes nobody. ::: ## Centering: move the zero to a meaningful place ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ncd <- ncd |> mutate(age_c = age - 50) # 0 now means "age 50" m_age_c <- lm(sbp ~ age_c, data = ncd) bind_rows(raw = tidy(m_age), centred = tidy(m_age_c), .id = "model") |> select(model, term, estimate) |> mutate(estimate = round(estimate, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 model term estimate 1 raw (Intercept) 96.3 2 raw age 0.74 3 centred (Intercept) 133. 4 centred age_c 0.74 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Slope unchanged** (0.74 mmHg per year) - **Intercept now = expected SBP at age 50** = 133 mmHg → interpretable - Centre on the **mean** or on a **clinically meaningful value** (age 50, BMI 25) ::: ## Same line, new origin ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s2_simple_regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ## Scaling: change the unit, not the relationship ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tidy(lm(sbp ~ I(age / 10), data = ncd)) |> select(term, estimate) |> mutate(estimate = round(estimate, 2)) # per 10 years ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 term estimate 1 (Intercept) 96.3 2 I(age/10) 7.43 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tidy(lm(sbp ~ scale(age), data = ncd)) |> select(term, estimate) |> mutate(estimate = round(estimate, 2)) # per 1 SD ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 term estimate 1 (Intercept) 132. 2 scale(age) 7.8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Per 10 years** reads naturally ("each decade of age adds …") - **Per SD** (standardised) lets you compare predictors measured in different units — but loses clinical units; prefer natural units for reporting ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 2 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `regression-workshop/labs/lab2_simple.R` - `lm()` · `summary()` · tidy coefficients - `predict()` with **both** interval types - Residual plot · R² · centred model ::: **Time:** 30 minutes · answer Q1–Q6 in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eyk5ww.mugnt1" data-show="RWFjaCBleHRyYSAxIGcvZGF5IG9mIHNhbHQgZ29lcyB3aXRoIDMuNCBtbUhnIGhpZ2hlciBt ZWFuIFNCUA==" data-explain="QSBzbG9wZSBpcyBhIGRpZmZlcmVuY2UgaW4gTUVBTiBvdXRjb21lIHBlciBvbmUtdW5pdCBk aWZmZXJlbmNlIGluIHRoZSBwcmVkaWN0b3IsIGluIG91dGNvbWUgdW5pdHMsIGFjcm9zcyBw ZW9wbGUuIEl0IGlzIGFuIGFzc29jaWF0aW9uLCBub3QgYSB3aXRoaW4tcGVyc29uIGNoYW5n ZS4="} The model sbp ~ salt_g gives a slope of 3.4. Which is the best interpretation? - Salt intake raises systolic pressure by 3.4 percent per gram - Each extra 1 g/day of salt goes with 3.4 mmHg higher mean SBP - Salt accounts for 3.4 mmHg of the SBP of each person studied - A person who adds 1 g of salt will see their SBP rise by 3.4 mmHg ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eykj5l.muh2ae" data-show="OTUlIHByZWRpY3Rpb24gaW50ZXJ2YWw=" data-explain="QSBwcmVkaWN0aW9uIGludGVydmFsIGFkZHMgdGhlIHBlcnNvbi10by1wZXJzb24gc2NhdHRl ciAocmVzaWR1YWwgU0QpIHRvIHRoZSB1bmNlcnRhaW50eSBpbiB0aGUgbGluZSwgc28gaXQg aXMgbXVjaCB3aWRlciB0aGFuIHRoZSBDSSBmb3IgdGhlIG1lYW4u"} A clinician wants the range within which the SBP of the NEXT patient eating 8 g/day is likely to fall. Which interval? - 95% confidence interval for the mean - 95% prediction interval - Standard error of the slope - Range of the sample ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eykweb.muhgrs" data-show="RXhwZWN0ZWQgbWVhbiBTQlAgYXQgYWdlIDUw" data-explain="Q2VudHJpbmcgbW92ZXMgdGhlIHplcm8gcG9pbnQ6IHRoZSBpbnRlcmNlcHQgYmVjb21lcyB0 aGUgZXhwZWN0ZWQgb3V0Y29tZSBhdCBhZ2UgNTAgd2hpbGUgdGhlIHNsb3BlIGlzIHVuY2hh bmdlZC4="} After centering age at 50 in `lm(sbp ~ age_c)`, what does the intercept represent? - SBP of a newborn - The change in SBP per year of age - Expected mean SBP at age 50 - The residual standard error ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q4" data-type="fill" data-hashes="6islbg.4p1n5e,21za2b.42nbp1,l03mr5.rr2h2l,6isl82.4p1n1u,fvk7tp.jy264x" data-show="MzA=" data-explain="QSBwcmVkaWN0aW9uIGludGVydmFsIGlzIGFib3V0IG1lYW4gwrEgMS45NiDDlyByZXNpZHVh bCBTRCwgd2hpY2ggaXMgMS45NiDDlyAxNSDiiYggMjkgbW1IZy4gVGhlIENJIGZvciB0aGUg bWVhbiBpcyBmYXIgbmFycm93ZXIu"} Residual SD is about 15 mmHg. A 95% prediction interval for ONE new patient is roughly the fitted mean plus or minus how many mmHg? (nearest 5) ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q5" data-type="fill" data-hashes="oxutpe.nl2erv,oxutsy.nl2evf,olub9w.pig92d,iv0m21.hqd4qd,ob4cr.t418wq" data-show="YWRqdXN0ZWQgcjI=" data-explain="QWRqdXN0ZWQgUsKyIGNoYXJnZXMgYSBwZW5hbHR5IGZvciBldmVyeSBleHRyYSBwYXJhbWV0 ZXIsIHNvIG5vaXNlIHZhcmlhYmxlcyBkbyBub3QgcmFpc2UgaXQgdGhlIHdheSB0aGV5IHJh aXNlIHBsYWluIFLCsi4="} Adding 20 pure-noise variables nudged R-squared up from 0.20 to 0.23. Which statistic should you read to judge whether they helped? (two words) ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **Slope** = change in mean outcome per 1 predictor unit — always say the **units** - **CI** → the mean; **PI** → an individual (always wider) - **OLS** minimises the sum of squared residuals - **R²** is descriptive; use **adjusted R²** to compare sizes; low R² ≠ unimportant - **Centre** so the intercept is meaningful; **scale** to a clinically sensible unit ::: **Next:** Session 3 — inference, confounding and multiple regression

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
